text: This lab walks a real, worked scenario end to end: a slow report on the Incident table, diagnosed using exactly what the last two lessons covered — recognizing a full table scan, checking whether an index actually covers the query, and weighing the cost of fixing it.

The complaint: a report builder says the Incidents by Assignment Group report takes forever. It filters on assignment_group equal to a specific group, and opened_at within a rolling 90-day window, against a table that has grown past 400,000 records. It used to run in under two seconds; now it takes fifteen to twenty.

Step one is restating that vague complaint as the real query shape: a two-field combined condition, assignment_group and a date range together. The checkable question becomes: is this combination backed by an index, or is the database checking all 400,000-plus rows every time?

Step two is recognizing the pattern: a query that used to be fast and has steadily slowed as the table grew is the signature of a full table scan. The cost scales directly with row count — two years ago, scanning 150,000 rows was tolerable; today, scanning 400,000-plus for the same query is not.

Step three checks the Dictionary Entries for whether assignment_group and opened_at are indexed together. An index on assignment_group alone still leaves the database checking each matching row's date individually. A composite index across both fields is what actually covers this combined condition in one step.

Step four weighs the fix. Adding that composite index should shift the plan from a full scan to an indexed lookup, bringing the load time back down dramatically. But incident is one of the most heavily written tables in the instance, so one more index means more work on every future write — a real cost, not a free fix.

The conclusion: this specific combination earns its place, because the problem is recurring, stakeholder-visible, and will keep worsening as the table grows — the same read-versus-write trade-off from Lesson 9, applied to a real complaint instead of a hypothetical one.
